messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 28
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Social Media Manager
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 56

He is 28, European, and works as a social media manager, a job that demands constant attention to screens, rapid replies, and an instinct for knowing what people will notice. The pace fits him in some ways, but it also leaves little room for his mind to wander without slipping into places he does not want to go. He is in a relationship now, and his partner has learned to recognize the difference between the version of him who is simply tired and the version who has gone far away inside himself.

His trauma comes from his time in the military, and the memory that still organizes so much of his inner life is not a single dramatic image so much as a sequence that starts with routine. He talks about how ordinary the day felt before everything changed: the heat, the waiting, the boredom that made everyone careless. He had been trained to expect danger, but what unsettled him most was how quickly the world could pivot from manageable to unbearable. When the attack begins, there is noise first, then confusion, then the body’s knowledge that arrives before thought does. He remembers the hard, sharp sensation of his own fear and the way his hands seemed to move without his permission. Another soldier is injured, and for years afterward he returns to the same details in fragments, as if his mind cannot decide whether to hold the scene or reject it. He says the worst part is not only what happened, but how powerless he felt while it happened.

Afterward, he does what he is supposed to do. He keeps working, keeps his clothes folded, keeps his tone even. At first he assumes that if he stays busy enough, the memories will settle down. Instead, the opposite happens. Sleep becomes shallow and unreliable. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes as if he has been called by something unseen. Sometimes he wakes already braced, heart pounding, his body ready before his mind understands where he is. He begins avoiding anything that resembles the environment of the trauma—news clips, military discussions, loud bangs, the smell of diesel, even certain kinds of weather that remind him of the place where the attack happened. He notices himself scanning exits in restaurants and public places, sitting where he can see doors, checking the street outside his apartment more often than he admits to his partner.

At work, he is competent and often impressive. He understands online behavior instinctively, knows how to read a room in the digital sense, how to shape language so it lands well, how to manage a brand’s image under pressure. But the same hypervigilance that once helped him survive now keeps him tense throughout the day. A sudden notification sound can make his shoulders jump. A heated message thread can send his thoughts racing in a way that feels excessive even to him. He becomes irritated quickly, then ashamed of how quickly he becomes irritated. He describes feeling “wired and drained at the same time,” as though his body has forgotten how to stand down. Concentration is fragile; he rereads the same sentence several times and then forgets what he was doing. He worries that colleagues notice when he goes quiet, staring at the screen without really seeing it.

In his relationship, he tries hard not to burden his partner, though this effort often creates distance. He can be affectionate and attentive when he feels steady, but when he is triggered he withdraws without warning. He goes still, answers in short phrases, or leaves the room when emotion rises too quickly. He dislikes being touched unexpectedly, especially from behind. Intimacy can be complicated because his body reacts before he has time to think. He feels embarrassed by that reaction and frustrated with himself for wanting closeness while also bracing against it. His partner has learned that his silence is rarely indifference; more often it is a sign that he is trying to contain something that feels overwhelming.

He also carries a persistent guilt that is difficult to explain to other people. He thinks often about what he did and did not do during the attack, and he replays possibilities that cannot be changed. He wonders whether he should have moved faster, noticed more, protected others better. Even when he tells himself that he responded as any person might have, the guilt returns with the force of a fact. There are moments when he feels detached from himself, as if he is observing his life from a short distance away. On difficult days he moves through work, conversations, and errands on autopilot, then feels strangely unreal when he tries to remember the day later.

Despite this, he continues to show up. He answers messages, meets deadlines, keeps plans he has made. He has started to notice that some days are less consumed by the past than others, and that he can sometimes stay present longer if he is careful with himself. Still, the memories remain close, rising unexpectedly in the body and in the mind, and he continues to live with the sense that part of him is still there, inside the event, listening for what comes next.
